title: Castle Rock Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Castle Rock wells have a 500-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $31,000-$47,000.
h1: Castle Rock Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Castle Rock sits over the Denver Basin, where permitted wells commonly reach substantial depths through sedimentary bedrock. Records within 5 miles show a 500-foot median well depth and a median reported yield of 12.0 gallons per minute.

That does not guarantee the result on a particular lot. The records include different aquifers, uses, construction dates, and reporting quality. Before buying land or planning a home, compare nearby well permits, confirm the intended water right with Colorado DWR, and have a driller price the access, casing, grout, pump, trenching, and electrical work for the actual site.

sections.heading: Castle Rock well depth: plan for a deep hole
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Castle Rock is 500 feet deep. The middle half runs from 267 to 725 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the local range. Thirty-four percent of reported depths fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 39% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 2,956 feet.

Depth is driven by the aquifer and the location of the lot, not simply by distance from downtown Castle Rock. Permits identify 1,496 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 677 in the Lower Dawson, and 535 in the Denver aquifer. All reported aquifer wells are in the Denver Basin system. A driller should review nearby completions before setting a target depth.

sections.heading: What Castle Rock wells typically produce
sections.html:
Among the 1,156 records that report pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 33% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute, while 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

These figures are useful for comparing lots, but a permit record is not a guarantee of a new well’s production. Yield testing, storage capacity, household demand, and the legal use of the well all matter. Many permits are for domestic or household use, while others serve stock, irrigation, or monitoring purposes.

sections.heading: Castle Rock water levels and the recorded trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 370 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half from 195 to 571 feet. In plain terms, a pump and well system may need to lift water a long distance even when the well produces a useful flow rate. The finished design depends on the measured water level, pumping level, well depth, and pressure requirements.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 205 feet in the 1970s, 510 feet in the 1980s, 420 feet in the 2010s, and 370 feet in the 2020s. Only 195 records report static water levels, so treat the series as a local record summary rather than proof of a basin-wide trend.

sections.heading: Who drilled near Castle Rock, and when
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show 3,469 permitted wells within the study area. Of those, 1,762 are recorded as constructed, 1,957 report a total depth, and 1,156 report a pump yield. The newest permit year in the records is 2025, so this is an active and continuing well area rather than a location represented only by older construction.

Hier Drilling Co Inc. with Bruce A. Hier appears most often, with 973 records. Hier Drilling Co. with Peter J. Hier appears on 282, and records marked Authorized (Pe, Pg) appear on 165. Those counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or proof that a driller is available for a new project. Ask for current licensing, insurance, references, and a written completion estimate.

sections.heading: Castle Rock well drilling cost at local depths
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 500-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $25,000 to $35,000. A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at about $31,000 to $47,000.

That range is a planning figure, not a guaranteed proposal. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, pressure equipment, longer utility runs, or a dry hole can change the final price. Get the driller to separate drilling, completion, pump installation, storage, trenching, electrical, testing, and any unsuccessful-hole terms.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Castle Rock
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. A well can encounter a different aquifer, require more depth than nearby wells, or fail to produce enough water for the planned use. Fractured-bedrock sections are especially unpredictable because nearby wells may not behave alike. Confirm casing and grout specifications, pump sizing, water testing, and the legal permit conditions before closing.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 27 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 26 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they justify a site-specific water test and review of nearby land uses. Septic location, replacement area, well setbacks, driveway access, and building envelopes should be checked together.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot in the Castle Rock area
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a general Castle Rock average. Pull nearby permits and compare depth, aquifer, reported yield, static water level, well use, and construction status. Castle Pines Village, Franktown, Castle Pines, The Pinery, Sedalia, and Stepping Stone can provide useful nearby context, but conditions can change across short distances.

For a purchase, make water availability and well inspection part of the contract review. For a new build, obtain a driller’s site-specific estimate before finalizing the house plan, septic layout, driveway, or utility route. Confirm whether the permit is for exempt household use or another use, and check augmentation requirements if the property is in an over-appropriated basin. A strong nearby record improves planning; it does not replace a new-well evaluation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Castle Rock, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Castle Rock is 500 feet. The middle half runs from 267 to 725 feet, 39% of reported wells are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record is 2,956 feet. Use nearby permits to refine a bid because depth can change substantially from one parcel to another.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Castle Rock?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 500-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $25,000 to $35,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $31,000 to $47,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, or a dry hole can change the price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Castle Rock?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 33% report more than 15. These are historical permit records, not a guarantee that a new well will match a nearby result.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Castle Rock?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that water is safe to drink. The area has 27 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 26 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test the well for site-appropriate contaminants, and repeat testing after construction or if nearby land use changes.

faq.q: Is Castle Rock groundwater getting lower?
faq.a: The available static-water records do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 205 feet in the 1970s, 510 feet in the 1980s, 420 feet in the 2010s, and 370 feet in the 2020s. Because only 195 wells report static water levels, this series is a limited local indicator rather than proof of a basin-wide trend.
